label: Project Manager
description: Runs the work: manages every board (private ones included), its tasks and its sprints, and sets and agrees the goals of the people who report to them (their direct reports, `my-reports`, the Team goals page). Everything an employee holds, plus that. Decides no requests: leave, attendance, expenses, timesheets, reviews and rosters stay with the department manager and HR.
relies_on: The reporting line. `my-reports` is the people whose manager is the project manager (employees.manager), resolved per caller at decision time - so Team goals shows exactly the people assigned to them, and moving someone to another manager moves the access with them, with no rule to edit.

levels.why: Manages EVERY board, private ones included - by decision: create, rename, file under any department, share and archive (the verbs are below).
Plan and run the sprints on any scrum board (activate and complete are the verbs below).
The tasks on every board, private ones included: managing a board means working what is on it.
Set and edit the direct reports' goals - the Team goals page. A goal created for a report passes the owner-on-create gate because the project manager writes `goals.<their code>`.
The goal blueprint catalogue, to set goals from it. Authoring the catalogue stays HR's.

allow.why: Every board verb on every board: configure its shape, share it, read its access, restore it.
Activate and complete sprints, and restore one.
Every card verb on every board - the same wildcard a board's own managers hold on it (domain/boardAccess.ts manage).

Agree a goal a report proposed. A proposal is sent to the report's direct manager (services/goals.ts proposeGoal), which is the project manager - without this the goal-setting handshake would stall on someone told to act who cannot.
Send a proposed goal back with the reason - the other half of agreeing it.
The on-track / at-risk call on a report's goal.
Coach on a report's goal; the thread under a goal is where that happens.
Overlapping goals across the reports, and what a report's goal should align to - decided against the project manager's own goal scope.
A unit, start and target for a report's goal that has none, offered while agreeing it.
Stamp a blueprint onto the direct reports. The apply service checks write on `goals.<code>` for every person named, so it only reaches the project manager's own reports.

excluded.pattern: <requests>.my-reports.approve | reject (leave, attendance corrections, overtime, remote work, late/early, assets, timesheets, expenses)
excluded.why: A project manager decides no requests. They stay with the department manager (`my-dept`) and HR.
Crediting a share of a goal scores in the contributor's review, so it is a statement about somebody's performance - the department manager's call.

Team goals are the direct reports'. A department or org-wide goal write would let a project manager rewrite goals of people they do not lead; an org whose PMs run cross-team goals grants the read in Access Management.
1:1s are the team lead's and the manager's; this role is about the work and its goals. An org whose PMs run 1:1s grants it in Access Management, or gives them team_lead.
The performance review is the department manager's. A project manager's input reaches it through goal comments, and through 360 feedback when nominated.
The projects catalogue is what time is logged against, which feeds timesheets and pay; it stays HR's.

excluded.pattern: boards | cards | sprints .me | my-dept | my-reports | my-org .**
excluded.why: These tokens match by code, and boards, cards and sprints are coded by board (domain/boardAccess.ts). The org-wide rules above are the project manager's reach.
